about: Analysis 2 is the Term 2 sequel to Analysis 1 (MATH0003) for first-year UCL Mathematics students (15 credits). The 2026–27 module description lists a rigorous theory of Riemann integration via upper and lower sums and the fundamental theorem of calculus, then improper integrals, Cauchy sequences, uniform continuity, L'Hôpital's rule, Taylor's theorem and power series in the complex plane. It is assessed by an 85% examination and 15% coursework, and you need at least 40% in the exam as well as overall to pass.

notes.h: Riemann integration via upper and lower sums
notes.body:
Analysis 2 opens by making "the area under a graph" precise. The approach is the Darboux form of the Riemann integral: trap the area between an overestimate and an underestimate and ask whether the two can be squeezed together.

Set-up (f bounded on [a, b])
- A partition P of [a, b] is a finite set of points a = x₀ < x₁ < … < xₙ = b. Write Δxᵢ = xᵢ − xᵢ₋₁.
- On each piece let Mᵢ = sup f and mᵢ = inf f over [xᵢ₋₁, xᵢ]. These exist because f is bounded.
- Upper sum U(f, P) = Σ Mᵢ Δxᵢ; lower sum L(f, P) = Σ mᵢ Δxᵢ. Always L(f, P) ≤ U(f, P).

Key lemmas
- Refinement: if Q ⊇ P (Q has extra points), then L(f, P) ≤ L(f, Q) ≤ U(f, Q) ≤ U(f, P). Adding one point splits one interval; the sup over each half is at most the old sup, so U cannot increase. The same argument with inf shows L cannot decrease.
- Any lower sum is at most any upper sum: L(f, P) ≤ L(f, P ∪ Q) ≤ U(f, P ∪ Q) ≤ U(f, Q).
- Hence the lower integral (sup of all lower sums) is at most the upper integral (inf of all upper sums).

Definition. f is Riemann integrable on [a, b] if its upper and lower integrals are equal; the common value is ∫ₐᵇ f.

Riemann's criterion. A bounded f is integrable if and only if for every ε > 0 there is a partition P with U(f, P) − L(f, P) < ε. This is the working test: you never need to compute the sup and inf over all partitions.

Standard examples
- f(x) = x on [0, 1] with the uniform partition into n pieces: U = (n + 1)/(2n) and L = (n − 1)/(2n). U − L = 1/n → 0, so f is integrable and ∫₀¹ x dx = 1/2.
- f(x) = x² on [0, 1]: U = (n + 1)(2n + 1)/(6n²) and L = (n − 1)(2n − 1)/(6n²), both → 1/3.
- Monotone functions are integrable: for increasing f and the uniform partition, the sum telescopes and U − L = (f(b) − f(a))(b − a)/n.
- Continuous functions on [a, b] are integrable. The proof uses uniform continuity (see that topic): choose δ so that |x − y| < δ gives |f(x) − f(y)| < ε/(b − a), then any partition with all Δxᵢ < δ has U − L < ε.
- The Dirichlet function (1 on rationals, 0 on irrationals) is not integrable on [0, 1]: every subinterval contains both kinds of number, so every U = 1 and every L = 0.

Properties you may quote once proved (f, g Riemann integrable on [a, b])
- Linearity: ∫(αf + βg) = α∫f + β∫g.
- Monotonicity: f ≤ g gives ∫f ≤ ∫g.
- Additivity: ∫ from a to c of f = ∫ from a to b of f + ∫ from b to c of f, for a < b < c.
- |f| is integrable and |∫f| ≤ ∫|f|; if m ≤ f ≤ M then m(b − a) ≤ ∫f ≤ M(b − a).
- Changing f at finitely many points changes neither integrability nor the value.

Exam tips: state Riemann's criterion exactly before you use it, write Mᵢ and mᵢ explicitly for your partition, and remember that discontinuity alone does not stop integrability (step functions are integrable).

The fundamental theorem links the integral built from upper and lower sums to differentiation from Analysis 1. It comes in two halves with different hypotheses, and exam questions often test exactly those hypotheses.

Part 1: the integral as a function of its upper limit
Let f be Riemann integrable on [a, b] and define F(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt.
- F is continuous on [a, b]. In fact, if |f| ≤ M then |F(x) − F(y)| ≤ M|x − y|, so F is Lipschitz.
- If f is continuous at a point c in (a, b), then F is differentiable at c and F′(c) = f(c).

Proof sketch of the derivative claim. For h ≠ 0,
(F(c + h) − F(c))/h − f(c) = (1/h) ∫ from c to c+h of (f(t) − f(c)) dt.
Given ε > 0, continuity gives δ with |f(t) − f(c)| < ε when |t − c| < δ. For 0 < |h| < δ the right-hand side has modulus at most ε. Hence the difference quotient tends to f(c).

Part 2: evaluating integrals with antiderivatives
If F is differentiable on [a, b] (one-sided at the ends) and F′ = f is Riemann integrable on [a, b], then ∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) − F(a).

Proof. Take any partition P. On each [xᵢ₋₁, xᵢ] the mean value theorem gives ξᵢ with F(xᵢ) − F(xᵢ₋₁) = f(ξᵢ)Δxᵢ, and mᵢ ≤ f(ξᵢ) ≤ Mᵢ. Summing, the sum telescopes: L(f, P) ≤ F(b) − F(a) ≤ U(f, P). This holds for every P, so F(b) − F(a) lies between the lower and upper integrals, which are equal.

Why the hypotheses matter
- In Part 1, continuity of f at c is needed. For the step function f = 0 on [−1, 0) and f = 1 on [0, 1], F(x) = ∫₋₁ˣ f = max(x, 0). F is continuous but has a corner at 0, so F′(0) does not exist even though f(0) = 1.
- In Part 2 we need F′ integrable; a function can have a derivative that is unbounded on [a, b] and therefore not Riemann integrable.

Consequences
- Integral mean value theorem: if f is continuous on [a, b], some ξ in [a, b] has ∫ₐᵇ f = f(ξ)(b − a) (apply the intermediate value theorem between the min and max of f).
- Integration by parts and substitution follow by integrating the product rule and chain rule, under continuity assumptions on the derivatives involved.
- Differentiating integrals with variable limits: if f is continuous and u, v are differentiable, then d/dx ∫ from u(x) to v(x) of f(t) dt = f(v(x))v′(x) − f(u(x))u′(x).

Worked example. d/dx ∫ from 0 to x² of cos(t³) dt = cos(x⁶) · 2x. And d/dx ∫ from x to x³ of e^{t²} dt = 3x² e^{x⁶} − e^{x²}. Both were checked numerically by finite differences.

Exam tips: always say which part you are using and check its hypothesis (continuity of f at the point, or integrability of F′); with variable limits, apply the chain rule to both limits and keep the minus sign on the lower one.

The Riemann integral needs a bounded function on a closed, bounded interval. Improper integrals extend it by taking limits when the interval is infinite or the function blows up at an end point.

Definitions
- Infinite range: if f is integrable on [a, R] for every R > a, then ∫ₐ^∞ f = lim as R → ∞ of ∫ₐᴿ f, when the limit exists (the integral converges).
- Unbounded integrand at a: if f is integrable on [a + ε, b] for each small ε > 0, then ∫ₐᵇ f = lim as ε → 0⁺ of ∫ from a+ε to b of f.
- Two-sided: ∫ from −∞ to ∞ converges only if ∫ from −∞ to 0 and ∫ from 0 to ∞ both converge separately. The symmetric limit of ∫ from −R to R (the principal value) is not the same thing: ∫ from −R to R of x dx = 0 for all R, yet ∫ from −∞ to ∞ of x dx diverges.
- An integral with several bad points is split so that each piece has exactly one.

Benchmark integrals (memorise)
- ∫₁^∞ x^(−p) dx converges if and only if p > 1, with value 1/(p − 1).
- ∫₀¹ x^(−p) dx converges if and only if p < 1, with value 1/(1 − p).
- ∫₀^∞ e^(−x) dx = 1; ∫₀¹ ln x dx = −1 (use x ln x → 0 as x → 0⁺).

Tests for convergence (f, g integrable on bounded subintervals)
- Comparison: if 0 ≤ f ≤ g on [a, ∞) and ∫ₐ^∞ g converges, then ∫ₐ^∞ f converges. Proof: R ↦ ∫ₐᴿ f is increasing and bounded above by ∫ₐ^∞ g, so it has a limit.
- Limit comparison: if f, g > 0 and f(x)/g(x) → L with 0 < L < ∞, the two integrals converge or diverge together.
- Absolute convergence implies convergence: 0 ≤ f + |f| ≤ 2|f|, so ∫(f + |f|) converges by comparison, and f = (f + |f|) − |f|.
- Integral test: if f is positive and decreasing on [1, ∞), then Σ f(n) and ∫₁^∞ f converge or diverge together. This shows Σ 1/nᵖ converges if and only if p > 1.

Worked examples
- ∫₁^∞ x^(−3/2) dx = [−2x^(−1/2)] from 1 to ∞ = 0 − (−2) = 2.
- ∫₀^∞ dx/(xᵖ(1 + x)): near 0 the integrand behaves like x^(−p), so we need p < 1; at infinity it behaves like x^(−p−1), so we need p + 1 > 1, that is p > 0. It converges exactly when 0 < p < 1. (For p = 1/2 the value is π, checked numerically.)
- ∫₂^∞ dx/(x(ln x)²): the antiderivative is −1/ln x, so the value is 1/ln 2.
- ∫₁^∞ (sin x)/x² dx converges absolutely, because |sin x/x²| ≤ 1/x² and ∫₁^∞ x^(−2) converges.
- ∫₁^∞ (sin x)/x dx converges (integrate by parts to get −cos x/x minus ∫ cos x/x², which converges absolutely), but it does not converge absolutely.

Exam tips: identify every bad point first and treat each separately; when comparing, compare with a power of x near the bad point; always state the inequality and its range of validity before quoting the comparison test.

notes.h: Cauchy sequences and the general principle of convergence
notes.body:
To prove a sequence converges from the definition you need to know its limit. Cauchy's idea removes that need: look only at how the terms behave relative to each other.

Definition. A real (or complex) sequence (aₙ) is Cauchy if for every ε > 0 there is N such that |aₘ − aₙ| < ε for all m, n ≥ N.

The main results, in the order they are proved
- Convergent implies Cauchy. If aₙ → a, choose N with |aₙ − a| < ε/2 for n ≥ N; then |aₘ − aₙ| ≤ |aₘ − a| + |a − aₙ| < ε.
- Cauchy implies bounded. Take ε = 1: for n ≥ N, |aₙ| ≤ |a_N| + 1, and only finitely many earlier terms remain.
- Bolzano–Weierstrass (from Analysis 1): every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence.
- A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges to the same limit. If a_{n_k} → a, choose K and N so that |a_{n_k} − a| < ε/2 for k ≥ K and |aₘ − aₙ| < ε/2 for m, n ≥ N; picking k ≥ K with n_k ≥ N gives |aₙ − a| < ε for n ≥ N.
- General principle of convergence: in ℝ, a sequence converges if and only if it is Cauchy. The same holds in ℂ, by applying it to real and imaginary parts.

Completeness matters. In ℚ the result fails: the decimal truncations 1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, … of √2 form a Cauchy sequence of rationals with no rational limit. The proof above uses Bolzano–Weierstrass, which rests on the completeness axiom of ℝ.

A common trap. |aₙ₊₁ − aₙ| → 0 does not make (aₙ) Cauchy. For aₙ = √n, consecutive gaps tend to 0 but aₙ → ∞. For the harmonic partial sums Hₙ = 1 + 1/2 + … + 1/n, we have H₂ₙ − Hₙ ≥ n · 1/(2n) = 1/2 for every n, so (Hₙ) is not Cauchy and diverges.

Contractive sequences. If |aₙ₊₂ − aₙ₊₁| ≤ k|aₙ₊₁ − aₙ| for all n with a fixed 0 < k < 1, then for m > n,
|aₘ − aₙ| ≤ Σ from j = n to m − 1 of |aⱼ₊₁ − aⱼ| ≤ (kⁿ⁻¹ + … ) |a₂ − a₁| ≤ kⁿ⁻¹|a₂ − a₁|/(1 − k),
which tends to 0, so (aₙ) is Cauchy and therefore converges. This is the standard way to handle recursively defined sequences such as aₙ₊₁ = 1/(1 + aₙ).

Cauchy criterion for series. Σ aₙ converges if and only if for every ε > 0 there is N with |aₙ₊₁ + … + aₘ| < ε for all m > n ≥ N. Consequences:
- aₙ → 0 is necessary for convergence (take m = n + 1).
- Absolute convergence implies convergence, because |aₙ₊₁ + … + aₘ| ≤ |aₙ₊₁| + … + |aₘ|.

Exam tips: when asked to prove a sequence is Cauchy, fix ε first, then produce an explicit N; to show a sequence is not Cauchy, exhibit an ε (often 1/2) and pairs m, n beyond any N with |aₘ − aₙ| ≥ ε.

Continuity at every point lets δ depend on both ε and the point. Uniform continuity asks for one δ that works everywhere at once, and this is what several later proofs (integrability of continuous functions in particular) need.

Definitions (f defined on a set A ⊆ ℝ)
- Continuous on A: for every x ∈ A and ε > 0 there is δ > 0 (allowed to depend on x) with |f(x) − f(y)| < ε whenever y ∈ A and |x − y| < δ.
- Uniformly continuous on A: for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that for all x, y ∈ A with |x − y| < δ we have |f(x) − f(y)| < ε. The order of quantifiers changes: δ is chosen before x and y.

Ways to prove uniform continuity
- Lipschitz functions: if |f(x) − f(y)| ≤ K|x − y| on A, take δ = ε/K. For f(x) = 3x + 1, δ = ε/3 works.
- √x on [0, ∞) is uniformly continuous although it is not Lipschitz near 0: |√x − √y| ≤ √|x − y|, so δ = ε² works.
- Heine–Cantor theorem: a function continuous on a closed bounded interval [a, b] is uniformly continuous there.

Proof of Heine–Cantor (by contradiction). Suppose not. Then there is ε₀ > 0 such that for each n we can find xₙ, yₙ ∈ [a, b] with |xₙ − yₙ| < 1/n but |f(xₙ) − f(yₙ)| ≥ ε₀. By Bolzano–Weierstrass some subsequence x_{n_k} → c, and c ∈ [a, b] because the interval is closed. Then y_{n_k} → c too. Continuity at c gives f(x_{n_k}) − f(y_{n_k}) → f(c) − f(c) = 0, contradicting the bound ε₀.

Ways to disprove it (sequential criterion)
f is not uniformly continuous on A exactly when there are ε₀ > 0 and sequences xₙ, yₙ in A with |xₙ − yₙ| → 0 but |f(xₙ) − f(yₙ)| ≥ ε₀ for all n.
- x² on ℝ: take xₙ = n + 1/n and yₙ = n. Then xₙ² − yₙ² = 2 + 1/n² ≥ 2.
- 1/x on (0, 1]: take xₙ = 1/n, yₙ = 1/(n + 1). Their difference tends to 0 but the values differ by 1.
- sin(1/x) on (0, 1): points where sin(1/x) = 1 and −1 get arbitrarily close near 0.

Useful facts
- A uniformly continuous function maps Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences. Since 1/n is Cauchy but 1/(1/n) = n is not, 1/x cannot be uniformly continuous on (0, 1].
- Closed and bounded are both needed in Heine–Cantor: x² fails on the unbounded set ℝ and 1/x fails on the bounded but not closed (0, 1]. On [0, 2], x² is uniformly continuous (it is Lipschitz with K = 4 there).
- Main application: every continuous function on [a, b] is Riemann integrable.

Exam tips: write the definition with quantifiers in the right order; for a counterexample give explicit sequences and the fixed ε₀; when using Heine–Cantor, say explicitly that the interval is closed and bounded.

L'Hôpital's rule evaluates limits of the indeterminate forms 0/0 and ∞/∞. In this module it is proved, not just used, and the proof rests on Cauchy's mean value theorem.

Cauchy's mean value theorem. Let f and g be continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b). Then there is ξ ∈ (a, b) with
(f(b) − f(a)) g′(ξ) = (g(b) − g(a)) f′(ξ).
Proof: put h(x) = (f(b) − f(a))g(x) − (g(b) − g(a))f(x). Then h is continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and a short calculation gives h(a) = h(b) = f(b)g(a) − f(a)g(b). By Rolle's theorem h′(ξ) = 0 for some ξ, which is the claim. Taking g(x) = x recovers the ordinary mean value theorem.

L'Hôpital's rule (0/0 form, one-sided). Suppose f and g are differentiable on (a, a + r) for some r > 0, g′(x) ≠ 0 there, f(x) → 0 and g(x) → 0 as x → a⁺, and f′(x)/g′(x) → L as x → a⁺ (L real, or ±∞). Then f(x)/g(x) → L as x → a⁺.

Proof. Define f(a) = g(a) = 0, so both are continuous on [a, x] for each x in (a, a + r). Since g′ ≠ 0, Rolle's theorem shows g(x) ≠ 0 there. Cauchy's MVT on [a, x] gives ξₓ ∈ (a, x) with f(x)/g(x) = f′(ξₓ)/g′(ξₓ). As x → a⁺, ξₓ → a⁺, so the right-hand side tends to L.

Variants with the same conclusion: two-sided limits, limits as x → ∞, and the ∞/∞ form (g(x) → ±∞), which needs a slightly longer proof.

Worked examples (each checked numerically)
- (1 − cos x)/x² → 1/2 as x → 0: one application gives sin x/(2x), a second gives cos x/2 → 1/2.
- (sin x − x)/x³ → −1/6: differentiate three times, getting (cos x − 1)/(3x²), then −sin x/(6x), then −cos x/6.
- x ln x → 0 as x → 0⁺: write it as ln x/(1/x), an ∞/∞ form; the derivative ratio is (1/x)/(−1/x²) = −x → 0. Hence xˣ = e^{x ln x} → e⁰ = 1.
- (eˣ − 1 − x)/x² → 1/2.

Ways to go wrong
- Using it when the form is not indeterminate: (x + 1)/(x + 2) → 1/2 as x → 0, but the derivative ratio is 1.
- Reading the theorem backwards. If f′/g′ has no limit, f/g may still have one. For x → ∞, (x + sin x)/x → 1, but (1 + cos x)/1 oscillates. Likewise x² sin(1/x) divided by x tends to 0 as x → 0, while the derivative ratio 2x sin(1/x) − cos(1/x) has no limit.
- Differentiating the quotient f/g with the quotient rule instead of differentiating f and g separately.

Exam tips: check and state the indeterminate form and the condition g′ ≠ 0 near the point each time you apply the rule; for products and powers (0 · ∞, 0⁰, 1^∞) rewrite as a quotient or take logarithms first.

Taylor's theorem says how well a polynomial built from derivatives at one point approximates a function nearby, with an explicit error term. Proving it with Cauchy's mean value theorem is a standard exam request.

Statement (Lagrange form). Let n ≥ 0 and x ≠ a. Suppose f⁽ⁿ⁾ is continuous on the closed interval between a and x and f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ exists on the open interval between them. Then there is ξ strictly between a and x with
f(x) = Σ from k = 0 to n of f⁽ᵏ⁾(a)(x − a)ᵏ/k! + Rₙ, where Rₙ = f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(ξ)(x − a)ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1)!.
The sum is the Taylor polynomial Pₙ of degree n about a.

Proof. Fix x. For t between a and x define
F(t) = f(x) − Σ from k = 0 to n of f⁽ᵏ⁾(t)(x − t)ᵏ/k!, and G(t) = (x − t)ⁿ⁺¹.
Differentiating F, the terms cancel in pairs (telescoping) and leave F′(t) = −f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(t)(x − t)ⁿ/n!. Also G′(t) = −(n + 1)(x − t)ⁿ, which is non-zero strictly between a and x. Note F(x) = 0, G(x) = 0, and F(a) = Rₙ. Cauchy's MVT on the interval between a and x gives ξ with
F(a)/G(a) = (F(x) − F(a))/(G(x) − G(a)) = F′(ξ)/G′(ξ) = f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(ξ)/(n + 1)!.
Multiplying by G(a) = (x − a)ⁿ⁺¹ gives the formula for Rₙ.

Applications
- Error bounds. Since the x⁴ coefficient of sin is 0, sin x = x − x³/6 + R₄ with R₄ = cos(ξ)x⁵/120, so |sin x − (x − x³/6)| ≤ |x|⁵/120. At x = 0.1: 0.1 − 0.001/6 = 0.0998333…, true value 0.0998334…, error about 8.33 × 10⁻⁸, within the bound 8.33 × 10⁻⁸.
- Approximating e: for 0 < ξ < 1, Rₙ = e^ξ/(n + 1)! < 3/(n + 1)!. With n = 5 the sum 1 + 1 + 1/2 + 1/6 + 1/24 + 1/120 = 2.71667, error 0.0016, within the bound 0.0042.
- Inequalities: with n = 1, eˣ = 1 + x + e^ξ x²/2 ≥ 1 + x for all real x.
- Higher-derivative test. Suppose f′(a) = … = f⁽ᵐ⁻¹⁾(a) = 0, f⁽ᵐ⁾(a) ≠ 0 and f⁽ᵐ⁾ is continuous at a. If m is even, a is a local minimum when f⁽ᵐ⁾(a) > 0 and a local maximum when f⁽ᵐ⁾(a) < 0. If m is odd, a is neither. Proof: f(x) − f(a) = f⁽ᵐ⁾(ξ)(x − a)ᵐ/m!, and by continuity f⁽ᵐ⁾(ξ) has the sign of f⁽ᵐ⁾(a) for x near a.
- Standard Maclaurin polynomials: eˣ ≈ 1 + x + x²/2 + x³/6; ln(1 + x) ≈ x − x²/2 + x³/3; cos x ≈ 1 − x²/2 + x⁴/24.

Taylor polynomial versus Taylor series. Rₙ → 0 is needed for the infinite series to equal f. The function f(x) = e^(−1/x²) (with f(0) = 0) has every derivative 0 at 0, so its Maclaurin series is identically 0 and equals f only at x = 0.

Exam tips: state the hypotheses (continuity of f⁽ⁿ⁾ on the closed interval, existence of f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ on the open one) and that ξ lies strictly between a and x; when bounding Rₙ, bound |f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾| over the whole interval, not just at a.

notes.h: Power series in the complex plane
notes.body:
The module ends by moving series into ℂ. A power series Σ aₙzⁿ (aₙ, z complex) behaves very simply: it converges inside a disc and diverges outside it.

Basic facts
- Absolute convergence (Σ |aₙ||z|ⁿ converges) implies convergence in ℂ, because ℂ is complete (the Cauchy criterion applies to real and imaginary parts).
- Key lemma: if Σ aₙwⁿ converges for some w ≠ 0, then Σ aₙzⁿ converges absolutely for every |z| < |w|. Proof: the terms aₙwⁿ tend to 0, so |aₙwⁿ| ≤ M for some M; then |aₙzⁿ| ≤ M|z/w|ⁿ, and the geometric series Σ |z/w|ⁿ converges since |z/w| < 1.

Radius of convergence. From the lemma there is R in [0, ∞], the radius of convergence, such that the series converges absolutely for |z| < R and diverges for |z| > R. On the circle |z| = R anything can happen.

Finding R
- Ratio method: if |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| → L, then R = 1/L (R = ∞ if L = 0, R = 0 if L = ∞).
- Root method (Cauchy–Hadamard, if lim sup has been covered in your course): 1/R = lim sup |aₙ|^(1/n). This works even when many coefficients are zero.
- Substitution: Σ z²ⁿ/4ⁿ = Σ (z²/4)ⁿ is geometric, converging when |z²/4| < 1, so R = 2. The plain ratio test on aₙ fails here because every other coefficient is zero.

Examples
- Σ zⁿ/n!: R = ∞. This defines exp z for all z ∈ ℂ.
- Σ n! zⁿ: R = 0; it converges only at z = 0.
- Σ n²zⁿ/3ⁿ: the ratio of coefficients tends to 1/3, so R = 3.
- Σ n! zⁿ/nⁿ: the ratio is (1 + 1/n)^(−n) → 1/e, so R = e.

Behaviour on the boundary (R = 1 in each case)
- Σ zⁿ diverges at every point of |z| = 1, because |zⁿ| = 1 does not tend to 0.
- Σ zⁿ/n diverges at z = 1 (the harmonic series) but converges at z = −1 (the alternating harmonic series, sum −ln 2).
- Σ zⁿ/n² converges absolutely at every point of |z| = 1, by comparison with Σ 1/n².

Functions defined by power series
- exp z = Σ zⁿ/n!, cos z = Σ (−1)ⁿz²ⁿ/(2n)!, sin z = Σ (−1)ⁿz²ⁿ⁺¹/(2n + 1)!, all with R = ∞.
- Splitting the exponential series into even and odd powers gives e^{iθ} = cos θ + i sin θ for real θ.
- The differentiated series Σ naₙzⁿ⁻¹ has the same radius of convergence, since n^(1/n) → 1. Inside the disc a power series can be differentiated term by term (quoted here; check whether your lecture notes prove this or just state it); for example d/dz exp z = exp z.

Exam tips: show the calculation that gives R and then test any boundary points asked about separately; for series with gaps (only even powers, say) substitute or use the root test rather than the coefficient ratio.

Adding points can only increase the lower sum and decrease the upper sum: L(f,P) ≤ L(f,Q) ≤ U(f,Q) ≤ U(f,P) when Q ⊇ P.
A bounded f on [a, b] whose upper integral (inf of all upper sums) equals its lower integral (sup of all lower sums).
Bounded f is integrable on [a, b] iff for every ε > 0 there is a partition P with U(f, P) − L(f, P) < ε.

questions.q: Let f(x) = x² on [0, 2] and let P split [0, 2] into 4 equal subintervals. What is the upper sum U(f, P)?
questions.why: f is increasing, so on each subinterval the sup is at the right end: (0.25 + 1 + 2.25 + 4) × 0.5 = 15/4. The value 7/4 uses left end points, which is the lower sum. 15/2 is the sum of the sups without multiplying by the width 1/2. 8/3 is the exact integral, which the upper sum only approaches as the partition is refined.

questions.q: Let f(x) = 1 if x is rational and 0 if x is irrational, on [0, 1]. Which statement is correct?
options: f is Riemann integrable with integral 0, because the rationals are countable
The upper integral is 1 and the lower integral is 0, so f is not Riemann integrable
f is Riemann integrable with integral 1, because every subinterval contains a rational
The upper integral is 0 and the lower integral is 1
questions.why: Every subinterval contains rationals and irrationals, so each sup is 1 and each inf is 0; every upper sum is 1 and every lower sum is 0, and these differ. The 'countable, integral 0' answer uses Lebesgue-integral reasoning, which does not apply to Riemann's upper and lower sums. The 'integral 1' answer looks only at the sups (the upper sums) and ignores the lower sums. An upper integral of 0 with a lower integral of 1 is impossible, since every lower sum is at most every upper sum.

questions.q: Using Riemann's criterion and the uniform partition Pₙ of [0, 1] into n equal pieces, prove that f(x) = x is integrable on [0, 1] and find ∫₀¹ x dx.
markScheme: States Riemann's criterion correctly
On [(i − 1)/n, i/n]: Mᵢ = i/n, mᵢ = (i − 1)/n (f increasing)
U − L = 1/n < ε once n > 1/ε, so f is integrable
Both sums → 1/2, so the integral is 1/2 (it lies between L and U for all n)
questions.modelAnswer: Riemann's criterion: a bounded f is integrable on [a, b] if and only if for every ε > 0 there is a partition P with U(f, P) − L(f, P) < ε. Take Pₙ = {0, 1/n, …, 1}. Since f is increasing, on [(i − 1)/n, i/n] the sup is i/n and the inf is (i − 1)/n. So U = Σ (i/n)(1/n) = n(n + 1)/(2n²) = (n + 1)/(2n), and L = Σ ((i − 1)/n)(1/n) = (n − 1)n/(2n²) = (n − 1)/(2n). Then U − L = 1/n. Given ε > 0 choose n > 1/ε; then U − L < ε, so f is integrable. The integral lies between L and U for every n, and both tend to 1/2, so ∫₀¹ x dx = 1/2.

questions.q: What is d/dx ∫ from x to x³ of e^{t²} dt?
questions.why: Write the integral as G(x³) − G(x) where G′ = e^{t²}; the chain rule gives 3x² e^{x⁶} − e^{x²}. Leaving out the factor 3x² (from differentiating x³) gives e^{x⁶} − e^{x²}. Adding the lower-limit term gets its sign wrong: the lower limit contributes −f(x)·1. Dropping the lower-limit term entirely gives 3x² e^{x⁶}, which treats the lower limit as a constant.

questions.q: Let f = 0 on [−1, 0) and f = 1 on [0, 1], and F(x) = ∫ from −1 to x of f(t) dt. Which statement is true?
options: F is differentiable at 0 with F′(0) = f(0) = 1
F is discontinuous at 0 because f jumps there
F′(0) = 1/2, the average of the one-sided values of f
F is continuous on [−1, 1] but not differentiable at 0
questions.why: F(x) = max(x, 0): it is continuous (indeed Lipschitz, since |f| ≤ 1) but has left derivative 0 and right derivative 1 at 0. Claiming F′(0) = f(0) applies FTC part 1 without its hypothesis that f is continuous at the point. Saying F is discontinuous confuses F with f: integrating smooths jumps. The value 1/2 averages the one-sided derivatives, but a derivative exists only when the two agree.

questions.q: State and prove the second part of the fundamental theorem of calculus (∫ₐᵇ F′ = F(b) − F(a)), stating clearly the hypotheses you use.
markScheme: Hypotheses: F differentiable on [a, b], F′ = f Riemann integrable
Takes an arbitrary partition and applies the MVT on each subinterval
Uses mᵢ ≤ f(ξᵢ) ≤ Mᵢ
Telescoping gives L(f, P) ≤ F(b) − F(a) ≤ U(f, P)
Concludes from equality of upper and lower integrals
questions.modelAnswer: Statement: if F is differentiable on [a, b] (one-sided at the end points) and f = F′ is Riemann integrable on [a, b], then ∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) − F(a). Proof: let P = {x₀, …, xₙ} be any partition. F is continuous on each [xᵢ₋₁, xᵢ] and differentiable inside, so the mean value theorem gives ξᵢ with F(xᵢ) − F(xᵢ₋₁) = f(ξᵢ)Δxᵢ. Since mᵢ ≤ f(ξᵢ) ≤ Mᵢ, summing gives L(f, P) ≤ Σ (F(xᵢ) − F(xᵢ₋₁)) ≤ U(f, P), and the middle sum telescopes to F(b) − F(a). So F(b) − F(a) is at least every lower sum and at most every upper sum, hence lies between the lower and upper integrals. As f is integrable these are equal to ∫ₐᵇ f, so ∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) − F(a).

questions.q: For which real p does ∫₀^∞ dx/(xᵖ(1 + x)) converge?
questions.why: There are two bad points. Near 0 the integrand behaves like x^(−p), needing p < 1; near infinity it behaves like x^(−p−1), needing p + 1 > 1, that is p > 0. Both must hold, so 0 < p < 1. The answer 'p < 1' checks only the end at 0, and 'p > 0' checks only the end at infinity. 'p > 1' applies the infinite-range test to x^(−p) instead of x^(−p−1), and also contradicts the condition at 0.

questions.q: What is ∫₁^∞ x^(−3/2) dx?
options: It diverges, since ∫₁^∞ x^(−p) dx only converges for p ≥ 2
questions.why: An antiderivative is −2x^(−1/2), which tends to 0 at infinity, so the value is 0 − (−2) = 2. Getting −2 comes from evaluating F(1) − F(∞), the limits the wrong way round. 2/5 comes from lowering the power to −5/2 (a differentiation-style slip) and dividing by −5/2. The divergence claim misremembers the benchmark: ∫₁^∞ x^(−p) converges for every p > 1, and 3/2 > 1.

questions.q: Which of these sequences is NOT Cauchy?
questions.why: √n is unbounded, so it does not converge and therefore is not Cauchy, even though √(n + 1) − √n → 0; small consecutive gaps are not enough. (−1)ⁿ/n tends to 0, so it is Cauchy; the alternating sign may make it look unsettled but the terms shrink. The partial sums of Σ 1/n² converge (p-series with p = 2), so they are Cauchy even though they keep increasing. 1/n converges to 0 and so is Cauchy.

questions.q: Which statement is correct?
options: A Cauchy sequence of rationals always converges in ℝ but need not converge in ℚ
Every bounded real sequence is Cauchy
A Cauchy sequence may have two subsequences with different limits
questions.why: ℝ is complete, so every Cauchy sequence of reals (rationals included) converges in ℝ; the limit can be irrational, such as √2. Small consecutive gaps do not give the Cauchy property: √n is a counterexample. Bounded sequences need not be Cauchy, for example (−1)ⁿ; Bolzano–Weierstrass gives only a convergent subsequence. A Cauchy sequence with one convergent subsequence converges to that limit, so all its subsequences share the same limit.

questions.q: Prove that every Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges. You may quote the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem.
markScheme: Shows Cauchy ⇒ bounded (ε = 1)
Applies Bolzano–Weierstrass to get a subsequence a_{n_k} → a
Chooses N from the Cauchy condition with ε/2 and K from the subsequence with ε/2
Picks k with n_k ≥ N and k ≥ K; triangle inequality gives |aₙ − a| < ε for n ≥ N
Concludes aₙ → a
questions.modelAnswer: Let (aₙ) be Cauchy. Bounded: with ε = 1 there is N₁ such that |aₙ − a_{N₁}| < 1 for n ≥ N₁, so |aₙ| ≤ max(|a₁|, …, |a_{N₁−1}|, |a_{N₁}| + 1) for all n. By Bolzano–Weierstrass there is a subsequence a_{n_k} → a for some real a. Now let ε > 0. Choose N with |aₘ − aₙ| < ε/2 for m, n ≥ N, and K with |a_{n_k} − a| < ε/2 for k ≥ K. Since n_k → ∞, pick k ≥ K with n_k ≥ N. Then for any n ≥ N, |aₙ − a| ≤ |aₙ − a_{n_k}| + |a_{n_k} − a| < ε/2 + ε/2 = ε. Hence aₙ → a.

questions.q: Which function is uniformly continuous on the stated set?
questions.why: |√x − √y| ≤ √|x − y|, so δ = ε² works everywhere; the unbounded slope at 0 does not stop uniform continuity. x² on ℝ is continuous, but continuity on an unbounded set is not enough: xₙ = n + 1/n and yₙ = n get close while their squares differ by more than 2. 1/x on (0, 1] lives on a bounded interval, but Heine–Cantor also needs it closed; 1/n and 1/(n + 1) get close while their images differ by 1. sin(1/x) is bounded, but boundedness does not help: it swings between −1 and 1 on ever shorter intervals near 0.

questions.q: For f(x) = 3x + 1 on ℝ, which choice of δ makes the definition of uniform continuity hold for every ε > 0?
questions.why: |f(x) − f(y)| = 3|x − y| < 3δ, which is at most ε exactly when δ ≤ ε/3. δ = 3ε inverts the factor and allows |f(x) − f(y)| up to 9ε. δ = ε ignores the factor 3 and allows differences up to 3ε. δ = (ε − 1)/3 subtracts the constant term, which cancels in f(x) − f(y), and is negative when ε < 1.

questions.q: Show that f(x) = x² is uniformly continuous on [0, 2] but not on ℝ.
markScheme: Gives δ = ε/4 (or cites Heine–Cantor correctly)
On ℝ: chooses xₙ = n + 1/n, yₙ = n (or similar)
Shows |xₙ − yₙ| → 0 but |xₙ² − yₙ²| = 2 + 1/n² ≥ 2
Concludes using the negation of the definition with ε₀ = 2 (or any ε₀ ≤ 2)
questions.modelAnswer: On [0, 2]: for x, y ∈ [0, 2], |x² − y²| = |x + y||x − y| ≤ 4|x − y|. Given ε > 0, take δ = ε/4; then |x − y| < δ gives |x² − y²| < ε, and δ does not depend on x or y. (Alternatively, x² is continuous on the closed bounded interval [0, 2], so Heine–Cantor applies.) On ℝ: let xₙ = n + 1/n and yₙ = n. Then |xₙ − yₙ| = 1/n → 0, but xₙ² − yₙ² = 2 + 1/n² ≥ 2. Take ε₀ = 2: for any δ > 0, choosing n > 1/δ gives points within δ whose images differ by at least ε₀. So no δ works for ε₀, and x² is not uniformly continuous on ℝ.

questions.q: What is lim as x → 0 of (sin x − x)/x³?
options: The limit does not exist, because the form stays 0/0 after one application of L'Hôpital
questions.why: Three applications give (cos x − 1)/(3x²), then −sin x/(6x), then −cos x/6 → −1/6 (equivalently sin x = x − x³/6 + …). 1/6 comes from a sign error in the cubic term of sin x. 0 comes from evaluating (cos x − 1)/(3x²) as 0 because its numerator is 0, but that is still a 0/0 form. A repeated 0/0 form just means you apply the rule again; it does not mean the limit fails to exist.

questions.q: What is lim as x → ∞ of (x + sin x)/x?
options: It does not exist, because (1 + cos x)/1 has no limit
questions.why: (x + sin x)/x = 1 + (sin x)/x, and |sin x/x| ≤ 1/x → 0, so the limit is 1. Saying 'does not exist' reads L'Hôpital backwards: the rule says that if f′/g′ has a limit then f/g has the same limit, not that f/g fails when f′/g′ does. The value 2 comes from evaluating 1 + cos x at x = 0 instead of taking a limit at infinity. The value 0 keeps only sin x/x → 0 and forgets that x/x = 1.

questions.q: Evaluate lim as x → 0⁺ of x ln x, justifying each step, and deduce lim as x → 0⁺ of xˣ.
markScheme: Rewrites as ln x/(1/x), an ∞/∞ form
Checks the derivative of 1/x is non-zero near 0
Derivative ratio (1/x)/(−1/x²) = −x → 0
Concludes x ln x → 0
xˣ = e^{x ln x} → e⁰ = 1 using continuity of exp
questions.modelAnswer: As x → 0⁺, x → 0 and ln x → −∞, so write x ln x = ln x/(1/x), which has the form −∞/∞. Both numerator and denominator are differentiable on (0, 1), and the derivative of 1/x is −1/x² ≠ 0 there. The ratio of derivatives is (1/x)/(−1/x²) = −x → 0. By L'Hôpital's rule (∞/∞ form), x ln x → 0. Then xˣ = e^{x ln x}, and since exp is continuous, xˣ → e⁰ = 1.

questions.q: Suppose f′(0) = f″(0) = f‴(0) = 0, f⁗(0) = −2, and f⁗ is continuous at 0. What is the nature of the point 0?
options: Nothing can be concluded without knowing the fifth and higher derivatives
A point of inflection, because f″(0) = 0
questions.why: Taylor's theorem gives f(x) − f(0) = f⁗(ξ)x⁴/24 with ξ between 0 and x; by continuity f⁗(ξ) < 0 near 0, so f(x) < f(0) and 0 is a local maximum. Calling it a minimum reverses the sign rule (negative even-order derivative gives a maximum). Calling it a point of inflection treats f″(0) = 0 as decisive, but the second-derivative test is just inconclusive there. Higher derivatives are not needed: the Lagrange remainder handles everything beyond the fourth-order term.

questions.q: What is the degree-3 Maclaurin polynomial of ln(1 + x)?
questions.why: The k-th derivative of ln(1 + x) at 0 is (−1)^{k+1}(k − 1)!, so the coefficient of xᵏ is (−1)^{k+1}/k: x − x²/2 + x³/3. Dividing by k! instead of k (as in the series for eˣ) gives x³/6. All plus signs is the series for −ln(1 − x). The constant term 1 is wrong because ln 1 = 0.

questions.q: Using Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange remainder, show that |sin x − (x − x³/6)| ≤ |x|⁵/120 for all real x, and hence give sin(0.1) correct to 6 decimal places.
markScheme: Notes the degree-4 Taylor polynomial of sin about 0 is x − x³/6 (x⁴ coefficient is 0)
R₄ = sin⁽⁵⁾(ξ)x⁵/5! = cos(ξ)x⁵/120
Uses |cos ξ| ≤ 1 to get the bound
questions.modelAnswer: sin is infinitely differentiable, so Taylor's theorem applies with n = 4 about 0. The derivatives of sin at 0 are 0, 1, 0, −1, 0, so the degree-4 Taylor polynomial is P₄(x) = x − x³/6. The remainder is R₄ = sin⁽⁵⁾(ξ)x⁵/5! = cos(ξ)x⁵/120 for some ξ between 0 and x. Since |cos ξ| ≤ 1, |sin x − (x − x³/6)| ≤ |x|⁵/120. At x = 0.1: P₄ = 0.1 − 0.001/6 = 0.09983333…, and the error is at most 10⁻⁵/120 ≈ 8.3 × 10⁻⁸. So sin(0.1) lies in [0.09983325, 0.09983342], giving sin(0.1) = 0.099833 to 6 decimal places.

questions.q: What is the radius of convergence of Σ from n = 0 of z²ⁿ/4ⁿ?
questions.why: The series is Σ (z²/4)ⁿ, a geometric series that converges exactly when |z|² < 4, so R = 2. The value 4 treats the series as if the powers were zⁿ rather than z²ⁿ. The value 1/4 takes the coefficient ratio 1/4 and forgets to invert it (and also ignores the even powers). The value 1/2 is lim sup |aₙ|^(1/n) = 1/2 from Cauchy–Hadamard, which equals 1/R, not R.

questions.q: How does Σ from n = 1 of zⁿ/n behave on the circle |z| = 1?
options: It converges at every point, since the terms tend to 0
It diverges at every point, since |z| = 1 is the boundary
It diverges at z = 1 and converges at z = −1
It converges at z = 1 and diverges at z = −1
questions.why: At z = 1 it is the harmonic series, which diverges; at z = −1 it is the alternating harmonic series, which converges (to −ln 2). Terms tending to 0 is necessary but not sufficient, as z = 1 shows. Being on the boundary decides nothing: behaviour on |z| = R must be checked point by point. Converging at z = 1 but diverging at z = −1 swaps the two cases.

questions.q: Find the radius of convergence of (a) Σ n²zⁿ/3ⁿ and (b) Σ n! zⁿ/nⁿ.
markScheme: (a) Ratio |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = ((n + 1)/n)² × 1/3
(a) Limit 1/3, so R = 3
(b) R = e
questions.modelAnswer: (a) aₙ = n²/3ⁿ, so |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = ((n + 1)/n)² · (1/3) → 1/3, and R = 3. (b) aₙ = n!/nⁿ, so aₙ₊₁/aₙ = (n + 1)! nⁿ/(n! (n + 1)ⁿ⁺¹) = (n + 1)nⁿ/(n + 1)ⁿ⁺¹ = (n/(n + 1))ⁿ = (1 + 1/n)^(−n) → e⁻¹. Hence R = e.

(a) A partition P of [a, b] is a = x₀ < x₁ < … < xₙ = b. With Mᵢ = sup and mᵢ = inf of f on [xᵢ₋₁, xᵢ] and Δxᵢ = xᵢ − xᵢ₋₁, U(f, P) = Σ MᵢΔxᵢ and L(f, P) = Σ mᵢΔxᵢ. The upper integral is the inf of U(f, P) over all P and the lower integral is the sup of L(f, P). f is Riemann integrable if these are equal, and ∫ₐᵇ f is the common value.

(b) Riemann's criterion: bounded f is integrable iff for every ε > 0 there is P with U(f, P) − L(f, P) < ε. Let f be continuous on [a, b] (so bounded, by the boundedness theorem). By Heine–Cantor f is uniformly continuous: given ε > 0 there is δ > 0 with |f(x) − f(y)| < ε/(b − a) whenever |x − y| < δ. Take any partition with every Δxᵢ < δ. On [xᵢ₋₁, xᵢ] the continuous f attains its sup and inf at points s, t of that interval, with |s − t| < δ, so Mᵢ − mᵢ = f(s) − f(t) < ε/(b − a). Then U − L = Σ (Mᵢ − mᵢ)Δxᵢ < (ε/(b − a)) Σ Δxᵢ = ε. By Riemann's criterion f is integrable.

(c) With xᵢ = i/n and f increasing on [0, 1], Mᵢ = (i/n)² and mᵢ = ((i − 1)/n)². So U = (1/n³) Σ from 1 to n of i² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/(6n³) = (n + 1)(2n + 1)/(6n²), and L = (1/n³) Σ from 0 to n−1 of i² = (n − 1)(2n − 1)/(6n²). Both tend to 2/6 = 1/3, and U − L = 1/n → 0. Since the integral lies between L and U for every n, ∫₀¹ x² dx = 1/3. (For n = 10: U = 0.385, L = 0.285.)

(d) Let G(y) = ∫₀ʸ cos(t³) dt. As cos(t³) is continuous, FTC part 1 gives G′(y) = cos(y³). The required function is G(x²), so by the chain rule its derivative is G′(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x⁶).

(a) Let n ≥ 0, a ≠ x, and suppose f⁽ⁿ⁾ is continuous on the closed interval I between a and x and f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ exists on its interior. Then there is ξ strictly between a and x with f(x) = Σ from k = 0 to n of f⁽ᵏ⁾(a)(x − a)ᵏ/k! + f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(ξ)(x − a)ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1)!.

(b) Fix x and for t ∈ I define F(t) = f(x) − Σ from k = 0 to n of f⁽ᵏ⁾(t)(x − t)ᵏ/k! and G(t) = (x − t)ⁿ⁺¹. Both are continuous on I and differentiable inside. Differentiating the k-th term of the sum gives f⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾(t)(x − t)ᵏ/k! − f⁽ᵏ⁾(t)(x − t)ᵏ⁻¹/(k − 1)! (the second part absent for k = 0); summing, everything cancels except f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(t)(x − t)ⁿ/n!. So F′(t) = −f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(t)(x − t)ⁿ/n!, and G′(t) = −(n + 1)(x − t)ⁿ ≠ 0 inside I. Also F(x) = 0 and G(x) = 0, while F(a) = Rₙ, the remainder we want. Cauchy's MVT gives ξ strictly between a and x with (F(x) − F(a))G′(ξ) = (G(x) − G(a))F′(ξ), that is F(a)G′(ξ) = G(a)F′(ξ). Hence Rₙ = F(a) = G(a)F′(ξ)/G′(ξ) = (x − a)ⁿ⁺¹ · f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(ξ)/(n + 1)!.

(c) For f = exp, every derivative is exp. With n = 1 about 0: eˣ = 1 + x + e^ξ x²/2, and e^ξ x²/2 ≥ 0, so eˣ ≥ 1 + x for all x (the case x = 0 is trivial). With n = 2: eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2 + e^ξ x³/6, and for x ≥ 0 the remainder is ≥ 0, giving eˣ ≥ 1 + x + x²/2.

(d) aₙ = 1/(n 2ⁿ), so |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = n/(2(n + 1)) → 1/2 and R = 2. At z = 2 the series is Σ 1/n, which diverges. At z = −2 it is Σ (−1)ⁿ/n, which converges by the alternating series test (the terms decrease to 0); its sum is −ln 2.
